title: The Floor She Consents To: Marie Taglioni, the Invention of Pointe, and the Shoes Left at the Wrong Grave
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Stockholm, the birth of a dancer's daughter
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In Stockholm a daughter is born to Filippo Taglioni, an Italian ballet master working the northern courts, and Sophie Karsten, a Swedish dancer and singer whose father Christoffer Christian Karsten is the great actor of the Royal Theatre. She is christened Marie Sophie. The trade she is born into runs deep on both sides of the house; her brother Paul will dance and choreograph beside her for forty years. Nobody in the family asks whether she will dance. The questions are where, and under whom, and at what age they start her.
suggested_refs: Parish and civic records of Stockholm for April 1804; the Karsten family of the Royal Swedish Opera

stops.name: Paris, the classes of Jean-Francois Coulon
stops.date_confidence: traditional; sources give only her childhood years in Paris, with no month or day
stops.campa: Her father sends her to Paris, into the classes of Jean-Francois Coulon, the teacher through whom half the Opera passes. What the Paris studios see is not promising: a rounded back, long thin arms, ankles judged too weak for the stamping brilliance then in fashion. One instructor is remembered asking whether that little hunchback will ever learn to dance. The remark survives with no document behind it, but the judgment it carries sits in every account of her girlhood. Her father takes her out of Coulon's hands and back into his own.
suggested_refs: The teaching lineage of Jean-Francois Coulon at the Academie Royale de Musique
sources: New World Encyclopedia, 'Marie Taglioni' (for the hunchback anecdote, unsourced)

stops.name: Vienna, six hours a day for six months
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the regimen is placed in 1822, immediately before the debut, without exact dates
stops.campa: Discouraged by what Paris has made of her, Filippo Taglioni carries his daughter to Vienna and sets her six hours a day for six months. He drills leg exercises and adagio positions, holding her in balance until the muscle gives out, and shows no sympathy for feet that bleed inside the shoes. He is not trying to make her resemble the dancers of the day. He is building a technique out of what she actually has: length, and a jump that comes down without sound. The bleeding feet come down to us from her biographers. She never wrote a line about these six months herself.
suggested_refs: Filippo Taglioni's training method, the 'level method' described in his biographies

stops.name: Karntnertortheater, the debut at eighteen
stops.date_confidence: attested; German Wikipedia gives 10 June 1822 at the Karntnertortheater, other summaries the year alone
stops.campa: At eighteen she walks onto the stage of the Karntnertortheater in a divertissement her father has made for her, dancing a nymph received at the court of Terpsichore. German playbills call the piece an Anacreontic divertissement and name her role Delia; French and English accounts render the same evening as La Reception d'une jeune nymphe a la cour de Terpsichore. Six months of Viennese drill stand behind the first entrance. What Vienna sees is a dancer who hangs a beat longer in the air than the music allows, and Vienna says so.
stops.quote: was born at Stockholm of an Italian father and a Swedish mother; she made her debut at Vienna in 1822, in a ballet composed by M. Taglioni expressly for his daughter.
stops.quote_source: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing, trans. Joseph Grego (London: Heinemann, 1898), chapter VI
suggested_refs: Playbills of the Karntnertortheater, Vienna, June 1822
sources: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing (1898)

stops.name: Munich, the Nationaltheater seasons
stops.date_confidence: contested: German Wikipedia places Munich and Stuttgart at 1825-1827, French Wikipedia at 1822-1826
stops.campa: She works the German court theatres in the years between Vienna and Paris. In Munich she dances at the Nationaltheater while her father negotiates the next engagement and the one after, building a reputation in cities where a ballerina can be seen and reported on without yet risking the verdict of the Paris Opera. The style he has built in her suits the German appetite for force no better than it will suit the French. He keeps her on these stages regardless, and no Paris critic sees her work until 1827.
suggested_refs: Repertory records of the Nationaltheater Munchen in the 1820s

stops.name: Stuttgart, the court theatre
stops.date_confidence: contested; the same 1822-1826 against 1825-1827 disagreement covers this engagement
stops.campa: At the Wurttemberg court theatre in Stuttgart she dances through the seasons her father arranges, one more provincial capital on the circuit that keeps the family fed and her technique in daily use. Some accounts make Filippo ballet master here; the standard list of his appointments names Stockholm and the Vienna Karntnertor and not this house. What is certain is that the pair are working, that the repertory is his, and that the floating jump and the soundless landing are drilled nightly in provincial houses, years before Paris sees either.
suggested_refs: Court theatre records of Stuttgart in the 1820s; the appointment list of Filippo Taglioni

stops.name: Kassel, the last of the German engagements
stops.date_confidence: contested; only French Wikipedia names Cassel, and its dating of the German circuit conflicts with the German account
stops.campa: Kassel, in the accounts that mention it at all, is the last of the German engagements before Paris. A single source names it, spells it Cassel, and gives years for the whole circuit that disagree with the years another source gives. The disagreement matters less than the shape: four or five years of court theatres, small houses, borrowed orchestras, a father calculating from the wings. Then the offer comes from the Academie Royale de Musique, and the provincial years end on a July afternoon.
suggested_refs: Hoftheater records of Kassel in the mid-1820s

segments.name: The Paris Opera, and the First London Season

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, the debut in Le Sicilien
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of July she enters the Salle Le Peletier in Le Sicilien, ou L'Amour peintre, a ballet by Anatole Petit into which her father has set a pas de deux for her alone. The Opera at this date rewards force: beaten legs, whipped turns, the visible labour of the athlete. She does none of it. She comes down out of a jump without a sound, holds a balance that appears to have no muscle in it, and within minutes the house understands that the terms have changed. She is engaged as a principal.
suggested_refs: Affiches of the Academie Royale de Musique, 23 July 1827

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, the six-year contract
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the contract is reported without a date in the sources consulted
stops.campa: On the strength of one afternoon Filippo Taglioni negotiates a six-year contract binding both of them to the Opera, father and daughter as a single instrument. He will make the ballets; she will be the reason to watch them. The arrangement gives him creative control over every role built around her, and gives her the only choreographer alive who knows what her body can be made to do. The terms are not preserved in anything reachable now, only the fact of the contract and the length of it.
suggested_refs: Contract registers of the Academie Royale de Musique, 1828

stops.name: King's Theatre, Haymarket, the first London season
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; Justin McCarthy gives 1829, and no month is recorded in the sources consulted
stops.campa: London gets her in 1829, at the King's Theatre in the Haymarket, the house that will become Her Majesty's once Victoria comes to the throne. The English response is the Parisian one at greater volume: a dancer who appears to have mislaid her weight. She will come back to this stage for the next eighteen years, and it is here, not in Paris, that she will finally stop. A historian of dancing, writing seventy years afterward, still needs a whole generation to say what the season did.
stops.quote: one of the most familiar names in the annals of the ballet, who turned the heads of an entire generation
stops.quote_source: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing, trans. Joseph Grego (London: Heinemann, 1898), p. 414
suggested_refs: Playbills of the King's Theatre, Haymarket, 1829 season
sources: Justin McCarthy, A History of Our Own Times, reprinted in Dance Index vol. 3, nos. 7-8 (1944), p. 119
Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing (1898), p. 414

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, the Ballet of the Nuns
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the third act of Meyerbeer's Robert le Diable the dead nuns rise out of their cloister graves and dance, and Marie Taglioni is the Abbess Helena who leads them. Duponchel and Ciceri have built a ruined moonlit convent to put them in. The scene turns the Paris stage toward the supernatural, and she dances it exactly six times before handing it to Louise Fitzjames, who will dance it two hundred and thirty-two. Her father opens La Sylphide on this stage four months later.
stops.quote: 'Have you seen Taglioni?' is the first question addressed to a stranger in Paris; and you hear her name constantly over all the hum of the cafes and crowded resorts of fashion.
stops.quote_source: N. P. Willis, Pencillings by the Way, reprinted in Dance Index vol. 3, nos. 7-8 (July-August 1944), p. 118
suggested_refs: Ciceri and Duponchel's cloister set for Robert le Diable, Act III, 1831

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, La Sylphide
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Her father builds a ballet around her and around nothing else: a Scottish farmhouse, a boy who abandons his wedding for a spirit only he can see, and a creature who cannot be held without dying of it. Marie dances the Sylphide, Joseph Mazilier the man who loses her, to Schneitzhoeffer's score and Adolphe Nourrit's libretto out of Nodier. Pointe work stops being a stunt on this night and becomes a claim about the body: a woman touches the floor because she consents to. Seventy-seven years on, Sergei Diaghilev will open a Paris season with a plotless white ballet named back at this one.
stops.quote: In Les Bayaderes and, above all, in La Sylphide, her art attained the utmost limits of spirituality.
stops.quote_source: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing, trans. Joseph Grego (London: Heinemann, 1898), p. 205
suggested_refs: The 1832 lithographs of Taglioni as the Sylphide; Schneitzhoeffer's autograph score
sources: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing (1898), p. 205

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, the skirt cut short
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: For the Sylphide she has her skirt cut to the calf, a white bell of gauze designed by Eugene Lami, so that the feet and the ankles can be seen doing what they do. Contemporaries find the exposure scandalous and copy it within a season. Hippolyte Lecomte had drawn the silhouette five years earlier for Pauline Montessu in La Somnambule; it is Taglioni who fixes it on the century, and the garment goes on being worn long after anyone remembers the ballet. Isadora Duncan will build an entire art out of refusing it.
suggested_refs: Eugene Lami's costume design for La Sylphide, 1832; Hippolyte Lecomte's 1827 design for La Somnambule

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, Le Dieu et la Bayadere seen by an American
stops.date_confidence: undated; Willis records the evening only as one of his Paris seasons in the 1830s, and the year here is a placeholder
stops.campa: An American traveller in Paris, filling the notebooks he will publish as Pencillings by the Way, buys a seat for Le Dieu et la Bayadere and finds his descriptive vocabulary will not reach. He is no balletomane and has no professional stake in the verdict. He writes down what the eye reports and gives up on explaining it, which is what most of Paris is doing this decade in worse prose. Her name, he notes elsewhere, is the first thing a stranger to the city gets asked about.
stops.quote: No language can describe her motion. She swims in your eye like a curl of smoke, or a flake of down. Her difficulty seems to be to keep to the floor.
stops.quote_source: N. P. Willis, Pencillings by the Way, reprinted in Dance Index vol. 3, nos. 7-8 (July-August 1944), p. 118
suggested_refs: N. P. Willis, Pencillings by the Way, the Paris letters

stops.name: London, the marriage to Gilbert de Voisins
stops.date_confidence: attested by German Wikipedia, which gives 18 September 1832 in London; English summaries give 1835 and place the wedding in France
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of September she marries Jean-Pierre-Victor-Alfred Gilbert de Voisins in London, six months after the Sylphide premiere and at the exact top of her fame. He is a count, thirty-two years old, and by every account uninterested in the discipline that governs her days. The German record gives date and city precisely; English summaries give 1835 and put the wedding in France, an error that has travelled a long way. The marriage lasts about three years in fact and twelve on paper.
suggested_refs: Marriage register, London, 18 September 1832

stops.name: Berlin, the Konigliches Opernhaus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Berlin appearances belong to the standard account of her touring circuit but no date was confirmed this session
stops.campa: Berlin takes her during the high decade, one stop on a circuit that now runs the whole of Europe: the German houses that trained a provincial girl receiving her back as the most expensive dancer alive. No source at hand fixes the dates or the programmes here; the Berlin appearances belong to the standard account of her circuit rather than to any document reached. The pattern behind them is the one her father set at Munich and Kassel and never dropped: keep her moving between capitals, so that no single audience grows accustomed to her.
suggested_refs: Repertory records of the Konigliches Opernhaus, Berlin, in the 1830s
sources: General accounts of Taglioni's touring circuit; not independently verified this session

stops.name: Paris, the marriage breaks
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Italian account dates the separation to roughly three years after the wedding, without a month
stops.campa: The marriage fails at about three years, on grounds the Italian account gives as infidelity and then leaves alone. Two children are born to it, of paternity disputed in some tellings; the son will marry into the Ralli money and the daughter will marry the Russian prince Alexander Trubetskoy. Marie keeps dancing throughout, four and five nights a week, in a costume built to make her look like something that has never had a body or a household. The formal divorce is nine years off.
suggested_refs: The Gilbert de Voisins family papers; the Ralli and Trubetskoy marriages of her children

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, leaving the Opera for Russia
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; the month of her departure is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: She leaves the Paris Opera in 1837 for a contract in Saint Petersburg. She is thirty-three, has held this house for a decade, and is going because Fanny Elssler is in it now, dancing the cachucha in a red skirt with a heat and a force that is everything Taglioni's style is defined against. Paris has spent three years being made to choose between them, in print, nightly, at length. The rivalry is the great subject of the ballet press of the 1830s, and sixty years later the two names are still set side by side.
stops.quote: After a feverish interval, while Napoleon's star faded on the horizon of the world, two planets rose in the firmament of Opera — Taglioni and Fanny Elssler. Other stars succeeded them, but never eclipsed their radiance.
stops.quote_source: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing, trans. Joseph Grego (London: Heinemann, 1898), Introduction, p. xv
suggested_refs: The Taglioni-Elssler partisan press of Paris, 1834-1837
sources: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing (1898), p. xv

stops.name: Bolshoi Kamenny Theatre, Saint Petersburg
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; a three-year contract, extended, with winter seasons running through 1842
stops.campa: She arrives in Saint Petersburg under contract to the Imperial Theatres and dances at the Bolshoi Kamenny, a house since pulled down, the Conservatory standing on its ground. The contract is written for three years and the winter seasons run five. What she meets in Russia is not admiration but something nearer a cult: balletomanes who attend every night of a run, who follow her carriage, who argue her technique in print with the seriousness of theologians. The Imperial school will teach her line for a century.
suggested_refs: Imperial Theatres contract records, Saint Petersburg, 1837; the site of the Bolshoi Kamenny, now the Conservatory

stops.name: Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Moscow appearances are reported in general accounts without dates or programmes
stops.campa: Moscow is said to have had her too, some season inside these five years, though no source consulted fixes the programme or the date. It is the kind of gap that opens around a career this large: the small provincial appearances get recorded and the obvious ones are assumed. She is by now the highest-paid performer in Europe and travels with her own repertory and her own conditions, and with a father in his sixties still setting the ballets she dances in.
suggested_refs: Imperial Theatres Moscow playbills, 1837-1842
sources: General accounts of her Russian tour; not independently confirmed this session

stops.name: The Moscow road, the bandits and the gold
stops.date_confidence: legend; no source fixes a date, and the coordinate marks a plausible midpoint of the road rather than an attested place
stops.campa: The story is told in every popular life of her and rests on nothing. Somewhere on the road between the two capitals her carriage is stopped by armed men who, recognising her, decline to rob her. They set a table upright in the road, or a plank across two stumps, and require her to dance; and when she has danced they pay her in gold and let her go on. No teller names a date, a place, or a witness. What the coordinate here attests is the shape of the legend and not the location of anything.
suggested_refs: The bandit anecdote as it circulates in popular Taglioni biography; no primary telling located
sources: Recurring ballet-lore anecdote; no primary documentation located this session

stops.name: Teatro alla Scala, Milan
stops.date_confidence: attested by Italian Wikipedia to the day
stops.campa: On the twentieth of May she makes her debut at the Teatro alla Scala, and Milan gives her the reception the rest of Europe has been giving her for fourteen years. Her father is Italian; this is a homecoming to a country she has never actually worked in. She is thirty-seven, an age at which the technique she invented costs her more than it did, and the notices do not mention it. The Milanese school has its own idea of virtuosity, harder and faster, and takes nothing from her but the shoes.
suggested_refs: La Scala playbills, 20 May 1841

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the shoes and the farewell
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of her last Russian season; the auction and the dinner are undated lore
stops.campa: She dances in Russia for the last time and the city loses its composure. A pair of her worn shoes is said to have been sold at auction for two hundred roubles; the same tellings go on to say the buyers cooked them, served them under a sauce, and ate them at a dinner in her honour. Neither half of this is documented anywhere. Both halves have been repeated for a hundred and eighty years, which is a fact about her audience even where it is not a fact about the shoes.
suggested_refs: The auctioned-shoes anecdote in the Russian balletomane literature; source untraced
sources: Wikipedia, 'Marie Taglioni', citing balletomane lore without an attributed primary source

stops.name: Paris, the divorce
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; no month or day in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The divorce from Gilbert de Voisins is made final twelve years after the wedding and nine after the marriage stopped working. She is forty, still dancing, and about to be put on one stage with the three women who have been described for a decade as her successors. Her private arrangements are by now Russian: the Trubetskoy connection runs through her daughter, and it will shortly put a palace on the Grand Canal into her hands. Money is coming in faster than anyone in the family is counting it.
suggested_refs: Divorce record of Taglioni and Gilbert de Voisins, 1844

stops.name: Her Majesty's Theatre, the Pas de Quatre
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Benjamin Lumley puts the four of them on his stage in one ballet: Taglioni, Carlotta Grisi, Lucile Grahn, Fanny Cerrito, with Jules Perrot choreographing four solos built to flatter each and rank none. Rehearsals nearly collapse over precedence until it is settled that they will appear in order of seniority, which puts Taglioni last, which is the answer she wanted. She is forty-one, and the rule that settles the quarrel is her age. A. E. Chalon draws the four of them together, and the lithograph outlasts every account of what the dancing looked like.
stops.quote_source: Verses by Theodore de Banville, quoted in Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing (London: Heinemann, 1898), p. 312
suggested_refs: A. E. Chalon's lithograph of the Pas de Quatre, 1845
sources: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing (1898), p. 312

stops.name: Her Majesty's Theatre, the Queen in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At the third performance the Queen and Prince Albert are in the house. The ballet has become the event of the London season within five days, and Lumley has found an audience that will pay to watch four rival women decline to destroy each other in public. Victoria is twenty-six and has held the throne since the year Taglioni left Paris for Russia. The Haymarket house changed its name for that accession; the dancer on its stage has been coming here since it was still the King's.
suggested_refs: Court circular records of the royal attendance, 17 July 1845

stops.name: Her Majesty's Theatre, the last entrance
stops.date_confidence: attested by German Wikipedia to the day; several summaries wrongly place the farewell in Paris
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of August she dances Le Jugement de Paris, Perrot's ballet to Pugni's score, at Her Majesty's Theatre, and then does not dance again. She is forty-three. The farewell is not in Paris, where the career was made, but in the London house that first took her in 1829, and it is quiet enough that later summaries put it in the wrong city and the wrong year. Twenty-five years of stage life close on an August evening in the Haymarket, in a role nobody now remembers.
suggested_refs: Playbill for Le Jugement de Paris, Her Majesty's Theatre, 21 August 1847

stops.name: Ca' d'Oro, Venice, the gift
stops.date_confidence: attested that Trubetzkoi bought the palace in 1846 and gave it to her; the year she takes up residence is not fixed
stops.campa: Prince Alessandro Trubetzkoi buys the Ca' d'Oro on the Grand Canal in 1846 and gives it to her. She retires into it: the most celebrated Gothic palace in Venice, its gold gone from the facade centuries ago, handed to a Swedish-born dancer forty-two years out of Stockholm. The connection runs through the Russian seasons and through her daughter's marriage into the same family. She did not buy the house and she does not restore it, which are the two things almost every later account says she did.
suggested_refs: Venetian property records for the Ca' d'Oro, 1846-1847

stops.name: Ca' d'Oro, the wellhead sold
stops.date_confidence: undated; the sales are attested, the individual years are not recorded in the sources consulted
stops.campa: What she does to the Ca' d'Oro is sell it off in pieces. The Bartolomeo Bon wellhead of red Verona marble goes, and carved features with it, lifted out of the courtyard and sold as architectural salvage. Baron Giorgio Franchetti will spend a fortune later undoing the work of these years, and the standard account of the palace calls the period a reckless renovation. The dates of the individual sales are not recorded. The building loses more to its famous tenant than to four centuries of water.
suggested_refs: The Bartolomeo Bon wellhead of the Ca' d'Oro, sold out of the courtyard and later recovered

stops.name: Blevio, the Villa Maria on Lake Como
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Italian local record names the villa for her without fixing the years of residence
stops.campa: At Blevio on the eastern shore of Lake Como there is a house the town still calls Villa Maria, after the ballerina who lived in it, raised out of an older building known locally as the Ca' dell'Imperatore. Trubetzkoy keeps his own villa on the same shore. She summers here in the years when the money is still arriving. The town keeps the name on the wall for the next century and a half, in the same years she is selling the Venetian palace off in pieces. Nothing in the local record says how she spent the days.
suggested_refs: Villa Maria, also called la Florida, at Blevio on Lake Como

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, inspectrice de la danse
stops.date_confidence: contested: summaries give the tenure variously as 1858-1870 and 1859-1870
stops.campa: She comes back to the Opera not to dance but to inspect: inspectrice de la danse, walking the classrooms, watching the corps at the barre, ruling on whether a girl of fourteen is being taught correctly. The technique she enforces is her father's, drilled into her in Vienna at a cost she never described in public and now written into the house standard. She holds the post until 1870. The summaries disagree by a year over when it begins, and none of them record what she was paid.
suggested_refs: Personnel registers of the Paris Opera ballet school, 1858-1870

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, the jury of the competition
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the date to the day appears in a single summary and is not corroborated
stops.campa: She sits on the jury of the first annual competition of the corps de ballet, judging the dancers of the house she took over thirty-three years earlier. The detail comes from one summary and carries a day and a month, which is more precision than its source can properly support. What it records is a woman of fifty-five inside the institution rather than on its stage, holding the power to advance or hold back girls born after she stopped performing.
suggested_refs: Records of the annual corps de ballet competition, Paris Opera, 1860

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, Le Papillon for Emma Livry
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She choreographs one ballet in her life and it is for Emma Livry: Le Papillon, to a score by Offenbach, about a girl turned into a butterfly and burned at a flame. Livry is twenty and has been dancing the Sylphide since 1858, the role Taglioni came out of retirement to coach her in. Everything the older woman knows is handed to the younger across two years of work. It is the only time she passes the technique on directly, and the subject she chooses is wings and fire.
suggested_refs: Offenbach's score for Le Papillon, 1860; the Livry costume plates

stops.name: Salle Le Peletier, the gauze catches
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At a rehearsal of Auber's opera La Muette de Portici, dancing the mime role of Fenella, Emma Livry's skirt passes over a gas jet in the wings and goes up. The gauze her teacher made fashionable is the most flammable garment on any stage in Europe, and Livry has refused the flameproofed version because it hangs badly and dulls the white. She is burned over most of her body and carried out of the theatre alive. Taglioni is fifty-eight and has spent two years making this girl the heir to everything.
suggested_refs: Accounts of the rehearsal fire of 15 November 1862 at the Paris Opera

stops.name: Paris, the death of Emma Livry
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Emma Livry dies eight months after the fire, of septicaemia, at twenty-one. The line that was to carry the Romantic technique into the next generation ends in a Paris sickroom. Taglioni will live another twenty-one years and choreograph nothing further. Le Papillon leaves the repertory with its dancer, and the ballet about a girl who flew too near a flame is not revived while anybody can be blamed for the coincidence. The house goes on using gauze.
suggested_refs: Emma Livry's grave at Montmartre; the flameproofing debate at the Paris Opera after 1862

stops.name: 14 Connaught Square, London, teaching deportment
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence, dated 1875-1876; the Italian account puts the move to London as early as 1871
stops.campa: The fortune is gone, on investments and family and the general collapse of a rentier's income, and at seventy-one she is in London teaching. From a house at 14 Connaught Square she gives deportment and social dancing to the daughters of fashionable families and takes a few private ballet pupils. Henri Bauer records her among English schoolgirls in Hyde Park. She is the last living person who danced the first Sylphide, and she is charging by the hour to teach girls how to enter a room.
suggested_refs: Henri Bauer's account of Taglioni teaching in Hyde Park, quoted by Vuillier
sources: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing (1898), p. 206

stops.name: Marseille, the house of her son
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year by the French account; no month recorded
stops.campa: At seventy-six she moves to Marseille to live with her son, which is the plain form of the sentence the French account gives: she can no longer keep herself. Georges Gilbert de Voisins takes her in. Forty years earlier the Imperial Theatres had paid her more than any performer in Europe, and Russian admirers were said to be eating her shoes with a sauce. She lives four more years in the south, in a city she never worked in, at the far end of a life that started in Stockholm.
suggested_refs: The household of Georges Gilbert de Voisins at Marseille, 1880-1884

stops.name: Marseille, death on the eve of eighty
stops.date_confidence: attested; English, French, German and Italian records all give 22 April 1884, and the 23 April variant in circulation is her own birth date
stops.campa: She dies in Marseille on the twenty-second of April, one day short of eighty. Four national records agree on the date; the twenty-third that circulates in some accounts is her own birthday, migrating across the page. She has outlived her father, her pupil Emma Livry, and the whole aesthetic she invented, which the Paris of 1884 regards as a period taste. A historian of dancing, writing fourteen years afterward, disposes of the ending in one line and does not soften it.
stops.quote: She died at Marseilles, very old and very poor.
stops.quote_source: Gaston Vuillier, A History of Dancing, trans. Joseph Grego (London: Heinemann, 1898), p. 206
suggested_refs: Death certificate of Marianne Sophie Taglioni, Marseille, April 1884

stops.name: Saint-Charles Cemetery, Marseille, the first grave
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the burial date is not recorded in the sources consulted and is placed a few days after the death
stops.campa: She is buried first in Marseille, in the cimetiere Saint-Charles, in the city where she died rather than any city where she worked. The plot is not identified in the sources consulted and the coordinate here marks the cemetery, not the grave. London notices the death: Justin McCarthy, writing a history of his own times, gives her a paragraph and dates the whole English enthusiasm back to a single season fifty-five years earlier. He calls her the most famous dancer that ever moved on a stage, and nobody in 1884 writes in to argue.
stops.quote: A few lines may be spared to chronicle the death in the same year (1884) of Madame Taglioni, the most famous dancer that ever moved on a stage. She made her first appearance in London in 1829, and all London and all England went wild over her, as the whole European continent had done.
stops.quote_source: Justin McCarthy, A History of Our Own Times, reprinted in Dance Index vol. 3, nos. 7-8 (July-August 1944), p. 119
suggested_refs: Burial registers of the cimetiere Saint-Charles, Marseille, 1884

stops.name: Pere-Lachaise, the ninety-fourth division
stops.date_confidence: undated; the French account records the transfer without a year, and it must postdate the Marseille burial
stops.campa: Her remains are moved to Paris and laid in the tomb of her grandson Auguste Gilbert de Voisins, in the ninety-fourth division of Pere-Lachaise. The French record states it plainly and gives the division. The English record still describes the burial place as debated, and the debate has never been formally closed. The transfer itself is undated in the sources reachable now. A dancer who defined one city's stage for twenty years ends with two graves in circulation and no agreement about which of them holds her.
suggested_refs: The Gilbert de Voisins tomb, Pere-Lachaise, 94th division

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, Petipa revives La Sylphide
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; no premiere date given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Marius Petipa mounts La Sylphide again for the Imperial Ballet, sixty years after the premiere and fifty after Taglioni last danced in Russia, with additional music by Riccardo Drigo. The ballet has outlived its dancer by eight years and will outlive its choreographer, its composer, and the empire paying for this revival. The white act, the gauze, the woman who cannot be held: the Petersburg audience of 1892 receives all of it as classical, which is what it was not in 1832.
suggested_refs: Riccardo Drigo's additional music for the 1892 Imperial Ballet La Sylphide

stops.name: Montmartre Cemetery, the shoes left at the wrong grave
stops.date_confidence: undated tradition; no origin date is reported, and the year here is a placeholder
stops.campa: Dancers begin leaving their worn pointe shoes at a grave in the Montmartre cemetery, in tribute to the woman who made the shoe expressive. The grave is very probably her mother's. English accounts still record the burial site as disputed between this cemetery and Pere-Lachaise; the French record gives Pere-Lachaise flatly. Nobody knows when the custom starts and nobody has managed to stop it, and the shoes go on accumulating against a stone under which she is almost certainly not lying. The tribute is exact about what it honours and wrong about where it is standing.
suggested_refs: The Montmartre grave associated with Taglioni and the pointe-shoe tribute

stops.name: Paris, Lacotte reads the ballet back out of the archives
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year
stops.campa: Pierre Lacotte works back through the archives to reconstruct the 1832 choreography and stages it in Paris, a hundred and forty years after the premiere and a hundred and twenty-five after its dancer left the stage. No original notation survives complete; the reconstruction is an argument built out of prints, memoirs, and the surviving Bournonville line in Copenhagen. What returns to a Paris stage is not her dancing. It is the best available reasoning about what her dancing must have been.
suggested_refs: Pierre Lacotte's 1972 reconstruction of the 1832 La Sylphide for the Paris Opera Ballet
